name: The missing middle
line: People went from hearing what it does straight to a blank prompt. The work was building the middle.
beats: “Today journey largely skips over middle, goes from ‘learn capabilities’ to ‘create’”
The middle has to show the system as accessible, give a reason to invest time, and build trust.
Explore, a page for each tool, and remix become the steps between.
alt: The journey model: states of mind from pre-discovery to creating a solution

name: Nobody starts from a blank page
line: New users will not write a prompt from nothing, so the first act became changing something that already exists.
beats: “We believe that new users will not be prepared to create from a blank prompt at first”
The research had a name for it: “Blank page paralysis”
“Remixing is the new creating”
alt: Hypothesis 7: Remixing is the new creating

name: A habit, not a blank slate
line: CodeWords replaces something people already do with a search, so the design has to beat a habit.
beats: “There are a variety of existing tools that are one google search away”
“a new way of completing an existing behavior to users, not a new behavior”
The test: do people who come for one tool branch into others?
alt: Hypothesis 1: Codewords requires a behavior change

name: Intent before curiosity
line: One rule settled most arguments: serve the person with a goal first, the browser second.
beats: “Favor people who have a goal to complete, and secondarily support people who are curious or idly browsing”
On a tool's page: “‘similar’ before ‘other’ because ‘Intent’ before ‘curiosity’”
Search turned down: “there is no point in replacing create with a far lower quality action”
alt: Hypothesis 3: Intent > Curiosity

name: Built for the few who go deep
line: A product for power users, dense on purpose, knowing most visitors never get that far.
beats: “Favor enabling power users over simplifying for casual users.”
“A small percentage of users will make it here.”
So the description, the detailed description and the spec all stay on the page.
alt: Hypothesis 4: Completeness over Simplicity

name: Eight bets, each with a way to be wrong
line: The deliverable was not screens. It was eight hypotheses, each with how to test it.
beats: Every slide: the bet, then “How to test”
“it is valuable to see if this hypothesis holds true”
The screens are the bets made visible.
alt: Hypothesis 2: There's a journey to adoption, with how to test it

name: The conversation is the onboarding
line: Instead of teaching the product first, the Architect teaches it while you build.
beats: “If you weren’t here to walk me through it, I would have dropped off already.”
So the walk-through became part of the product: an Architect you can ask anything.
“Major focus should be on the architect, and speaking to it”
alt: The Architect answering a question in the build screen

name: Nothing arrives finished
line: Making a tool went from one shot to a draft you keep working on.
beats: “Ideas rarely show up fully formulated.”
“iterative rather than “one and done””
A spec that stays editable, a history of builds, one spec to many tools.
alt: Hypothesis 6: Draft state matters

name: Who decides, the person or the machine
line: Two bets pull against each other, and one Review button holds both.
beats: “We will look to the user for confirmation on the AI’s work”
“Optimize for giving users something they can use, over getting into the details of how its going to be done”
“I did not modify the new prompt because I was scared to break anything.” Review proposes; you accept or edit.
alt: Hypothesis 5: Defer to the human

name: Trust is spent before it is earned
line: Every dead end costs trust, so the design's first job is to stop wasting it.
beats: “Trust built w/ user needed this journey to happen”
What to avoid: “Losing information / context the user has shared”
A failed run, in the research: “feels like a dead end”
alt: The run page: the steps of a run, its output, and similar tools

name: What is a function?
line: The product's own words were the first wall: people did not know what a function or an integration was.
beats: “Create a function that... I don’t know what a function is.”
“these arent AI tools though. They are tools made with AI.”
The box on the landing page asks for a tool, not a function.
alt: The old flow with what the user is thinking at each step

name: One line, many tries
line: The headline was worked like a design problem: candidate after candidate until one could carry the product.
beats: “AI-tools. For every Job.”
“Generated tools.”
“Outsource to AI.” and under it “The code to bring your words to life.”
alt: Headline candidates on the wireframe board

name: A model in the head at every step
line: Each screen was judged by one question: what does the person now believe is happening?
beats: The loop every screen has to close: “User action”, “System state change”, “Feedback for state change”, “User mental model update”
During a build: “Do I just sit and wait?”
At the output: “MIssing end point (what do i do with this now?)”
alt: The audit of the old product's structure, with the feedback loop

name: Consumer, remixer, builder, chainer
line: The product is a staircase, and each page is a step up it.
beats: “Tool consumer”, “Tool remixer”, “Tool Builder”, “Tool Chainer”
Run a tool, then change one, then write your own.
The top step: “a sub-function for another codewords function”
alt: The builder personas board

name: An argument in sticky notes
line: The product was designed as a conversation between two people, five rounds of it, on one board.
beats: Round one: “How is explore different from the main page?”
Round four: “is this intent and curiosity? how are we grabbing intent”
Round five: the Architect page appears.
alt: Wireframe round four, with the sticky-note thread

name: Two doors, one room
line: Exploring and creating started as separate flows. The work was joining them.
beats: “Explore flow” and “Create flow”
“need to figure out how these two flows can merge together”
Customize on any tool opens the Architect with that tool's prompt already filled in.
alt: The two flows: explore and create

name: Five tools that make the case
line: The landing page argues with examples: each tool on it was picked for the feeling it sets off.
beats: “Feels hard to do with available tools”
“it should be easy and free and here it is”
“If we could give the user any way to be wow-ed in their first experience”
alt: The landing page

name: What we said no to
line: The product is as much the things turned down as the things built.
beats: Search: “the team doesnt want to prioritize search”
Free runs: “no point in getting a person to “run” if they dont want to commit”
The community user: “at the moment we dont need to design for that”
alt: Wireframe round three
from: Wireframe rounds 3 and 4 · User journey board

name: When there is nothing to show
line: Most of the design is for the cases where something is missing: no description, no author, no credits.
beats: “If author not defined, use “Codewords””
“If no description, how do we fail gracefully?”
“Fail case for running out of credits. Where? On run? on use?”
alt: The last wireframe round, with the list of edge cases
from: Final UI, the notes beside the screens

name: The wait
line: A build takes time, and nobody knew what to do while it ran.
beats: “Things are happening. But how long should I wait for?”
“The information is too subtle.”
The build log names who is working: “Architect: Planning high level steps”
alt: The old flow for building a new function, with its build stages
from: CodeWords UX board · user research · wireframe round 5

name: Told before you spend
line: Whether a tool can be built should be known before the build, not after it.
beats: “Ideally the user should know before they even approach this stage.”
“It has told me before I’ve spent any credits attempting to build it which is nice”
Review moves that answer into the conversation, before Build.
alt: The scope of work, page by page

name: A page for a thing that did not exist
line: A generated tool needs a product page: what it does, proof that it works, what to do with it.
beats: “built in 48 seconds” and “run 300 times”
Use the spec, get the API, get the code, or just run it.
“we should show the most similar functions, always”
alt: A tool's page: built in 48 seconds, run 300 times

name: The feature they already loved
line: Users loved one thing in the old product. The redesign made it the whole product.
beats: “The prompt helper is genius.”
“They love “Check & Enhance Prompt” but...”
The Architect: “wokrs like check and enhance today but better characterization of the dialog”
alt: The Architect page: the conversation on the left, the spec and the build on the right

name: Speed is the promise
line: What the team is good at is speed, so speed is what the product says and shows.
beats: “I think this team has speed as a strength and iteration as a strength.”
“instead of “create software” it is “create software faster””
On every tool: “generated in x seconds, the equivalent of y dev hours”
alt: Hypothesis 8: Users want it done
from: User journey board · wireframe round 3 · hypothesis 8

name: In, out, steps
line: One grammar runs from the first box to the last page: what goes in, what comes out, the steps between.
beats: “Describe the inputs, outputs and steps.”
Tools sorted by what they turn into what: “okay i think input->output better ;-)”
The spec, the build and the run page all read Input, Steps, Output.
alt: Wireframe round two, with the first spec pages
